newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Housing, jobs key to Bosnia reconstruction - minister.
newsitem.headline: Housing, jobs key to Bosnia reconstruction - minister.

text.p: Housing and jobs are the cornerstones of reconstruction efforts in Bosnia-Herzegovina, an international donor conference was told on Thursday.

"If you have a home and a job, you have something that is a clear sign of normality in your community," said Bosnian Trade Minister Hasan Muratovic. "These are the key aspects of rebuilding our country.
Muratovic was speaking at a news conference during a two-day international donor meeting on Bosnia-Herzegovina which opened on Thursday.
Sponsored by the World Bank and the European Commission, the conference seeks to examine projects to attract aid totalling $5.1 billion over three years to help rebuild the war-ravaged federation.

World Bank officials said the international community had already pledged over $1.8 billion to Bosnia in 1996, of which $1.2 billion had been allocated to specific projects and some $720 million dispersed.
Bank official Christine Wallich told the news conference that $1.4 billion would be needed for 1997.

She said the bank also wanted to see more finance available to the Serb Republic provided it made progress in living up to the terms of Dayton peace agreement that ended 43 months of war in late 1995.
Officials have said just two percent of the available aid has gone to the Serb Republic, nine percent to the Bosnian Croats and the remainder to the rest of Bosnia.
But officials said this should not be taken as a sign of "punishing" the Serb Republic for its percieved blame in the conflict.

"To some extent the allocation reflects the degree with which authorities are abiding by the terms of the Dayton accords," one bank official said. "To a greater extent, however, the allocation reflects the degrees of destruction and reconstruction in various areas."
The Brussels meeting aims to identify key areas and projects for international investment ahead of a donors pledging conference to be held later this year.

World Bank officials said they wanted to see some emphasis shift towards encouraging more private investment in the area, even to the extent of underwriting guarantees in the event of hostilities resuming.

"Five years ago if you looked at any country in eastern Europe and asked which one was closest to Western-styled economic markets and practices the answer would have been Yugoslavia," said one bank official.
"However, today the situation is such that Albania is probably in a better position than what remains of Yugoslavia."
Muratovic said not one single industry or enterprise remained in Sarejevo -- particularly hard-hit during the conflict -- and enormous problems were being faced by local people.
"But there has been progress," he said. "We have been rehousing, we have been resettling refugees ... we are even exporting electricity."

Rebuilding institutions such as the central bank, telephone companies and social security systems was a key test of seeing just how prepared the various communities were to work together, Muratovic said.
He said he believed the will existed to make it a success.
